groups.instructions: Read the passage about a market's quiet-hour trial and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
At Cedar Quay market, Saturday mornings used to be filled with music from speakers, shouted prices and delivery carts. Some residents enjoyed the lively atmosphere, but others avoided the market because the combined noise felt overwhelming. After several discussions, the market association agreed to test a quiet shopping hour, from eight to nine on Saturday mornings, for six weeks.

During that hour, stallholders switched off background music, lowered their voices and displayed price lists in large print. Staff also received guidance on giving customers enough time to ask questions. The association explained that the aim was to make shopping more comfortable for people who found loud environments difficult, while keeping the market open to everyone.

A fruit seller initially worried that the quieter atmosphere would reduce sales. On the first two Saturdays, fewer people visited during the early hour than during the following hour, but those who came often stayed longer and asked more detailed questions. Because the numbers were small and the weather differed between weekends, the association refused to announce that quiet hours had increased or decreased sales.

One problem occurred when a refrigerated delivery cart arrived at 8:15 and made a loud noise near the entrance. The market manager arranged for routine deliveries to happen after nine, while allowing urgent deliveries of medical supplies at any time. At the end of the trial, visitors could submit suggestions in writing or speak to a volunteer. The association planned to review all comments before deciding whether the quieter hour should become a permanent feature.

options.text: On Fridays from seven to eight.

options.text: All shoppers left after five minutes.

options.text: The delivery drivers asked for longer holidays.

options.text: Whether the quiet hour raised or lowered sales.

options.text: It considered the trial successful before gathering feedback.

groups.instructions: Read the passage about the school ecology club's lighting study and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
Along Oakridge Lane, the lights outside several shops remained bright throughout the night. An ecology club at a nearby school noticed that few moths were visiting the flowers beside the pavement, although a retired gardener remembered seeing many more years earlier. The students wondered whether the direction of artificial light could be one factor.

Instead of asking businesses to turn off their lights, the club proposed fitting simple shields to lamps on one side of the lane. The shields directed light towards the ground rather than into the surrounding trees. For four weeks, students observed moths near shielded and unshielded lamps at the same hours, taking photographs from marked positions. They also recorded temperature and rainfall because both could influence insect activity. No insects were handled or collected.

Heavy rain interrupted observations in the first week. Later, shopkeepers expressed concern that the shields might make the path unsafe. The students measured how well the pavement was lit and added small reflective strips near a sharp corner. They found that the pavement remained visible, although one shop entrance needed its lamp adjusted.

By the end of the study, the students had counted more moth visits near the shielded lamps on most dry evenings. However, they knew that different flowers had opened at different times during the month, making it difficult to attribute the change to lighting alone. Their report explained this limitation and recommended repeating the study over several seasons. The town council thanked the club for combining environmental questions with attention to the safety of pedestrians.

options.text: Whether the direction of night lighting might affect moth visits.

options.text: To identify individual insects by name.
